Charlie the Elephant | Journey to Shamballa

By: Joy Summers | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Charlie, South Africa's loneliest zoo elephant, in captivity for 42 years, starts his new life at Shamballa private nature reserve

Unique Selling Point:
Footage shot by Greg of the entire process of moving Charlie - and almost exclusive access

Summary:
After almost 40 years in captivity, Charlie, the lone elephant at the National Zoo in Pretoria is embarking on a new life in the Shamballa private reserve near Vaalwater.
Summary
Charlie was captured in Hwange over 40 years ago and trained in the Boswell Wilke Circus. When the circus closed down, he was transferred to the Natal Lion Park and then in 2001 to the Pretoria Zoo. He has been in captivity for 42 years.

In 2022 the government announced their desire to retire Charlie who has gained celeb status as one of the loneliest elephants in South Africa. The EMS Foundation answered the call and have spent millions on the mammoth operation. They have appointed a specialist team made up of South African and international elephant specialists both medical and behavioral to assist them with his relocation and his rehabilitation into a natural protected area.


Further information:
A special crate was built for Charlie, and for the last couple of weeks he has been habituated to the crate. The idea was to allow Charlie to set the pace. The team want to use as few drugs as possible due to his age. Today he will begin the 3-hour journey to Shamballa where his new elephant handlers await him. It’s not without risk and the team are cautiously confident he will make the journey without incident.

Carte Blanche tells the story of this former circus elephant, who has spent the last two decades in a zoo but will finally know freedom for the rest of his days. It will also question if it’s worth it to spend so much on a lone old elephant. Behind the scenes, this relocation has also been fraught with red tape.

Script:


Charlie’s journey to Shambala - FINAL SCRIPT FOR VO

TITLE: 23rd July 2024 National Zoo, Pretoria

Voice over 1
A hive of activity at an elephant enclosure at the Pretoria Zoo, as a team of welders hastily construct a metal safety wall.

Up sound welding - Masks and sparks

Man
They say we have 3 hours, Charley in enclosure here and a little bit of stress involved

Voice over 2
While the welders work, a lone bull elephant is confined to his night quarters

Dr Marina Ivanova
International Mission Co-ordinator Four Paws
With all this noise around he is curious, who are you? Where is my food, why don't I get my food, because usually now its the small brunch before the lunch

Voice over 3
The elephant hasn't always trusted human’s and so the barrier is critical for safety.

Dr Peter Rogers
Four months ago he was restless and unpredictable. I got a big fright … I turned away and he slapped me on the shoulder

Voice over 4
A specialised team must now train this animal to walk into a specially designed crate….the first step in a complex process

It's taken almost two years of planning, it's no small operation and its not without risk

Voice over 5
This is the story of Charlie, the last remaining elephant at the National Zoo, and his journey back into the wild

FADE TO BLACK


Up sounds of capture

LINK CLAIRE
Charley was about 2 years old when he was captured in Hwange and the sounds of the bush were replaced by drum rolls and applause.

Up sound circus

Voice over 5
Charley had become a circus elephant. And this was his life for at least 18 years

Up sound circus with music and noise etc

To this day he has never forgotten those circus tricks

Up sound circus and clowns

Voice over 6
In 2001 the zoo became Charlie’s new home in Pretoria and he has been here for the last 23 years.

He has had several companions over the past two decades, but the last died in 2020 and he has been alone ever since

Link
In 2021, 42 000 people signed a petition to free Charley and a groundbreaking decision was made by government to retire him from the national Zoo

Voice over 7
Human and animal rights group- the EMS foundation, has put together a team.

Up sound

Megan Carr leads the project

Megan Carr
Its a first for Africa, that a government has offered retirement ….so that is an unbelievable step for our country ….and then the logistics team

Voice over 8
The crate, custom designed for Charlie, has to fit snuggly with no sharp edges into this space.


Dereck Milburn
it's a matter of centimetres to get it fitted. Charlie doesn't like steps so we are trying to get it perfectly level

Voice over 9
Dereck Milburn’s organisation, We Wild Africa is supporting logistics and providing Charley’s food- a vital part of his training.

Dereck Milburn
Charlie loves Paw paw, so there was a lot of pawpaw flying into the zoo/ basically he eats four bales of teff a day/ and the challenging fact was really getting browse he loves acacia.. not much so we fed him Karee and jobs created

Voice over 10
Over 24 hours, Charlie eats 50 kilograms of a cereal called teff, 15 kilograms of fruit and vegetables, 7 kilograms of so-called boskos, 50 kilograms of natural browse -and one loaf of bread!

Voice over 11
The team thought it might take months for Charlie to get used to the crate, but the day after it arrives his curiosity gets the better of him

He gingerly tests the floor …

And lured by an out of reach apple, he takes a tentative step inside

Mathias Otto is the head trainer

Mathias Otto
I speak with him and make a little bit noisy on the metal that he understands ok that is not a bad thing/ and yes when he goes backwards I close the doors and he can see oh those are doors and they close/ And I think that was a good first session.

Voice over 12
The training involves touching Charlie lightly with bamboo rods, then a click and reward when he responds correctly to an instruction

Damaged by years in captivity, his feet will need future care, so he’s trained to lift them for easier treatment in his new home.
Voice over 13
But the training’s primary focus is ensuring Charlie gets used to the crate in preparation for his upcoming journey. If he falls, he could suffocate.

And just three days later, Charlie astonishes everyone when he walks confidently inside.

Megan
An elephant that in the past had been aggressive to humans, suddenly trusted humans

“What's that’’

Claire
We can't not talk about the costs involved, so where is the money coming from?
Megan
So the EMS has sponsored the entire project. its an enormous amount of money massive investment…for rest of his life …and many people said he was going to fail, that he would never walk into a crate

Voice over 14
While Megan wades through a mountain of permits, Charlie is given an unusual gift: the dung from different elephants from what it’s hoped will be his new home in Limpopo

PAUSE

That’s where Shadrack Ndlovu will be monitoring him.

Shadrack
For me to take dung just to give him a warning he might meet other elephants ..there's something coming along

Voice over 15
By mid August Charlie is ready to leave, but Zoo workers worry that losing their star attraction will cost them their jobs.

Megan Carr
We are not willing to sit here and pay another R500 000 and take the abuse. We won't do it. Why will we?

Voice over 16
The trucks are turned back, costs are rising and the delays put the project in jeopardy

Megan Carr up sound
Today or we are going to reconsider everything that is all there is to it

Voice over 17
Charlie’s freedom hangs in the balance

FADE TO BLACK

TITLE: MONDAY 19th AUGUST 2024

Voice over 18
It's five days later and the zoo is still blocking the trucks from entering. But the team is determined that, no matter the obstacles, Charlie will leave today.

Dr Amir Khalil
What we hear now and this is surprising, the engineer of the zoo has to examine the cars. I don't understand why. but now we have pressure because the elephant has had some medication and time is very important now

Voice over moved
A light sedative has been hidden in his banana bread.

The permits are all in place and Charlie is ready

Dr Frank Goeritz
Good morning Charlie

Voice over 19
But will this captive elephant finally be free

Doors close up sound

Up sound Jawol good zu!

Voice over 20
By 9am, Charlie has been in his crate for 90 minutes waiting for a crane now held up at the gate.

Dr Frank Gouritz
So we are waiting for the crane, so we have problems getting into the zoo I guess

Voice over 21
So how do you keep an elephant in a small crate calm?

Dr Amir singing
My friend

You sing Frank Sinatra’s My Way, of course.

Voice over 22
It’s Dr Amir Khalil’s signature tune. He’s director of the global animal welfare organisation, Four Paws, and has overseen many animal relocations, including other elephants, from some of the world’s most hostile places.

Dr Amir Khalil
I have very ugly voice but one time I started to sing for myself /and I notice the elephant has tears in his eyes and it’s the first time in my life I have such experience. / and this starts every day and the elephant calms down…music food for the soul

Up sound singing …HEY CHARLIE GOOD BOY

Voice over 23
Three hours later, after a few last-minute snacks - 5.5 tonnes of mildly sedated elephant lifts off the ground.
Dr Frank Goeritz is head vet

Dr Frank Goeritz
When we started moving he got stressed out so we gave him a bit of sedative so he calmed down now. I guess he is ready to hit the road now

Voice over 24
But the staff, still angry that Charlie is leaving, don't want the truck to go.

Up sound
Charlie is our bread and butter. Amandla!

Voice over 25
The vets monitor Charlie on cameras mounted inside the crate. Thankfully, he’s calm but tensions are rising.

Megan Carr
You know we had overcome so much by the time we were rolling out of that zoo, that the protest was there and it happened, but it didn't stop us.

Up sound Charlie!

Voice over 26
It’s sunset by the time Charlie arrives at his new home in Limpopo: Shambala.

Up sound crane not level - whoa stop!

Voice over 27
Charlie has been in his crate for around ten hours and he wants out

He’ll stay in this Boma for about ten days for safety,

But on his first evening in the bush he begins communicating with elephants over the rise

FADE TO BLACK HERE

Voice over 28
Earlier this month, Charlie was released from the boma into a smaller section of his new 24 hectare rehabilitation home.

Megan Carr
He is very brave, walked out of his enclosure of his own accord, into the first field of freedom

Voice over 29
It’s time to leave behind his old circus name, and his African elephant handlers have given him a new one - Duma - or thunder

Dr Peter Rogers
As he came out he grabbed a big clump of grass and put it in his mouth and then he went straight to the mud

Voice over 30
It's spring, and after 42 years in captivity - this magnificent creature is finally at home in his new mud pool in the African bush.

Dr Peter Rogers
It gave me goose pimples, this is like a dream come true for him.
Megan
It was all that we all needed, to see that he was in the right place

THE END

PROMO ONE
Voice over
In a first, the South African government gives the go ahead to retire Charlie the lone bull elephant at the National Zoo

Megan up sound
Charlie had to be trained to walk into a crate, / they said he would never walk into a crate, so yes we took a huge leap of faith

Voice over
But not everyone wanted the elephant to leave

Up sound protest





PROMO TWO

Voice over
How to calm an elephant by singing Frank Sinatra’s My way

Dr Amir Singing

Voice over
The mammoth undertaking of training a 5 tonne bull elephant to walk into a crate so he can be transported into his new home

Up sound of the transport and loading


PROMO THREE
Voice over
Captured as a young elephant, Charlie became a circus performer for almost 18 years, then he was given to the National Zoo

Derek Milburn up sound
Charlie loves paw paw …as long as you need the byte

Voice over
Now 42 years later a team of animal lovers are reintroducing him slowly into the wild

CORRECT STRAPLINES:
Dr Marina Ivanova
International Mission Co-ordinator Four Paws

Dr. Peter Rogers
Supervising Wildlife Veterinarian

Dr Frank Goeritz
Head Veterinarian: Leibniz- IZW

Megan Carr
EMS Project Lead: Towards Freedom

Dr. Amir Khalil
Director: Four Paws International


Shadrack Ndlovu
Head Elephant Monitor: Shambala Private Game Reserve


Dereck Milburn: Director: We Wild Africa

Summary Charlie was captured in Hwange over 40 years ago and trained in the Boswell Wilke Circus. When the circus closed down, he was transferred to the Natal Lion Park and then in 2001 to the Pretoria Zoo. He has been in captivity for 42 years. In 2022 the government announced their desire to retire Charlie who has gained celeb status as one of the loneliest elephants in South Africa. The EMS Foundation answered the call and have spent millions on the mammoth operation. They have appointed a specialist team made up of South African and international elephant specialists both medical and behavioral to assist them with his relocation and his rehabilitation into a natural protected area.
metadata.Further information: A special crate was built for Charlie, and for the last couple of weeks he has been habituated to the crate. The idea was to allow Charlie to set the pace. The team want to use as few drugs as possible due to his age. Today he will begin the 3-hour journey to Shamballa where his new elephant handlers await him. It’s not without risk and the team are cautiously confident he will make the journey without incident. Carte Blanche tells the story of this former circus elephant, who has spent the last two decades in a zoo but will finally know freedom for the rest of his days. It will also question if it’s worth it to spend so much on a lone old elephant. Behind the scenes, this relocation has also been fraught with red tape.
